title: Data Mining and Its Limits
blurb: What counts as a pattern, descriptive vs. predictive models, and why looking in enough places always finds something.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Data mining is finding patterns in data that are valid (they hold on new data), useful (you can act on them), unexpected (not already obvious) and understandable (people can read them).
  • Descriptive or predictive? Ask one question: is there a column you are trying to predict? No outcome column: descriptive (association rules, clustering). An outcome column: predictive (regression for a number, classification for a category).
  • Bonferroni's principle. Look in enough places and you will find something, even in pure noise. Test 20 things at the 5% level and about one will "work" by chance.
  • Rhine's paradox. Guessing all 10 red/blue cards right happens with probability 1/210 = 1/1,024. Test about 1,000 people and about one "psychic" appears. Retest with new cards and they score about 5 of 10, like everyone else. Our ESP Test did the same thing on purpose.

steps.title: Patients with similar symptoms
steps.prompt: A hospital has symptom records for 50,000 patients but no diagnosis column. It wants to find groups of patients whose symptoms look alike. What kind of data mining is this?
options: Descriptive: there is no column to predict
Predictive: it predicts each patient's diagnosis
Predictive: it predicts which group a patient belongs to
Neither: data mining needs an outcome column
steps.why: There is no outcome column, so this is descriptive data mining (clustering). Predicting needs a column to predict, such as a diagnosis that is already recorded for past patients.

steps.title: Loans that default
steps.prompt: A bank has 200,000 past loans, each marked defaulted or repaid. It wants to flag new applications that look likely to default. What kind of data mining is this?
options: Predictive: classification, since the outcome is a category
Predictive: regression, since the outcome is a category
Descriptive: association rules
Descriptive: clustering
steps.why: The defaulted/repaid column is the outcome, so this is predictive. The outcome is a category, so it is classification. Regression predicts a number, such as the amount still owed.

steps.title: How many 'psychics' by luck?
steps.prompt: A lab asks 8,000 people to call 10 hidden cards, red or blue. Nobody has ESP. About how many will call all 10 right by luck alone?
options: about 0.8
about 8
about 80
about 800
none: 10 in a row by chance is impossible
steps.why: 8,000 × 0.5<sup>10</sup> = 8,000 / 1,024 ≈ 7.8, so about 8. The chart above shows the same thing with 2,000 people: about 2. Look at enough people and someone gets lucky.

steps.title: Forty subject lines
steps.prompt: A marketing team tests 40 different email subject lines, each against the usual one, and reports the one that raised clicks "significantly" (at the 5% level). Use Bonferroni's principle to explain why this result may not be a real finding, and what the team should do before acting on it.
hints: At 5% each, how many of 40 would 'win' with no real effect at all?
What did the lab do with its psychics, and what happened?

title: The Data Mining Process: CRISP-DM
blurb: The six steps, why most of the time goes to the first three, and why fitting the model is the easy part.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• CRISP-DM (CRoss-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) has six steps: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation, deployment.
  • It is a cycle, not a line. The arrows go back: modeling often sends you back to data preparation, and evaluation can send you back to business understanding.
  • Most of the time goes to steps 1 to 3. Understanding the client's real goal, understanding the data, and getting it in shape: Phases I and II of this course. Step 1 was Flight Plan's lesson: solve the problem the client actually has.
  • Data mining is hard because of scale, many columns (Job Scout alone has 139 skills), mixed data, poor data quality, data spread across owners, and privacy. Fitting the model is the easy part once the data is understood and in shape.

steps.title: Right before modeling
steps.prompt: In CRISP-DM, which step comes right before modeling?
options: business understanding
data understanding
data preparation
evaluation
deployment
steps.why: The order is business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, then modeling. Data preparation (cleaning, joining, reshaping) gets the data into the shape the model needs.

steps.title: The model misses the goal
steps.prompt: A team's model scores well on accuracy, but in the evaluation step the client says it does not answer the question the business needed. Where does CRISP-DM send the team?
options: Back to business understanding
On to deployment, since the accuracy is good
Back to modeling, to try a bigger model
Nowhere: the process ends after evaluation
steps.why: CRISP-DM is a cycle. A model that misses the business goal sends you back to step 1: understand the real question first.

steps.title: "Let's skip to the model"
steps.prompt: Your manager says: "Let's skip ahead and start modeling the job postings today. The model is where the value is." Using CRISP-DM, explain where most of the time in a data mining project goes, and why skipping ahead is risky.
hints: Which three steps come before modeling?
What could go wrong if nobody checked the goal or the data first?

title: Frequent Itemsets and A-Priori
blurb: Support, frequent itemsets, and the monotonicity idea that lets A-Priori skip most of the counting.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Baskets and items. A basket is one trip to the store (or one job posting); its items are what it holds (or the skills it asks for).
  • Support of an itemset is how many baskets hold the whole set. It can be a count (2 baskets) or a share (2 of 5 = 0.4); R's arules reports the share.
  • Frequent itemset: support at or above a threshold s that you choose.
  • Monotonicity. A set can appear in no more baskets than each of its parts. So if an item fails the threshold, every set that holds it fails too, and A-Priori never counts those sets. Pass 1 counts single items; pass 2 counts only pairs of frequent items.

steps.title: Count the pairs
steps.prompt:
Six baskets and four items; a filled dot means the basket holds the item. With a support threshold of 3 baskets, which of these pairs is frequent?
breadmilkeggsbutter
B1●●●○
B2●○○●
B3○●●○
B4●●○●
B5○○●●
B6●●○○
options: {bread, milk}
{milk, eggs}
{bread, butter}
{eggs, butter}
none of these pairs
steps.why: {bread, milk} is in B1, B4 and B6: 3 baskets. {milk, eggs} and {bread, butter} are in 2 each, and {eggs, butter} in 1. Count the rows that have both dots.

steps.title: Groceries: an item that fails pass 1
steps.prompt: We run A-Priori on R's Groceries data (9,835 baskets) with support = 0.01, so an itemset needs at least 99 baskets. In pass 1, {mayonnaise} appears in 90 baskets. In pass 2, what happens to the pairs that contain mayonnaise?
options: A-Priori never counts them
A-Priori counts them, since pass 2 counts every pair of items
A-Priori counts only those whose other item also appears in fewer than 99 baskets
A-Priori counts them, and keeps those that appear in at least 90 baskets
A-Priori counts only those with a confidence of at least 0.5
steps.why: Monotonicity: a pair with mayonnaise can appear in at most 90 baskets, below 99, so it can never be frequent. A-Priori skips it without counting, and the same goes for pairs with any other item below 99. Confidence plays no part in counting itemsets. (If you run it, the log says "Absolute minimum support count: 98": 0.01 × 9,835 = 98.35, so an itemset still needs 99 baskets.)

steps.title: Why skip the pair?
steps.prompt: Explain in your own words why A-Priori never counts a pair that contains an item that failed the support threshold in pass 1.
hints: Can {A, B} show up in a basket that does not hold A?
If the item is below s, where does that leave the pair?

title: Association Rules in R
blurb: Confidence and lift in plain words, reading arules output, and mining rules from R's Groceries data in your browser.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• A rule I → j: people who buy everything in I often buy j too.
  • Confidence: of the baskets that hold I, the share that also hold j. It is the conditional probability P(j | I).
  • Lift: how many times more likely j is in a basket with I than in any basket: confidence / P(j). A lift of 1 means I tells you nothing about j; below 1, j is less likely with I. High confidence alone is not a finding when j is in most baskets anyway.
  • Reading arules::inspect(): support is the share of baskets with every item in the rule; confidence as above; coverage is the share of baskets with the left side; count is the number of baskets with every item, left and right.

The class code, on R's Groceries data (one month of a grocery store, 9,835 baskets, 169 items). Nothing is loaded: every call names its package.

data('Groceries', package = 'arules')

arules::summary(Groceries)
arules::itemFrequency(Groceries) |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(10)

grocery_rules = arules::apriori(
  Groceries, parameter = list(
    support = 0.01, confidence = 0.5, minlen = 2)  )

arules::summary(grocery_rules)
arules::sort(grocery_rules, by = 'count', decreasing = TRUE)[1:3] |> arules::inspect()

steps.title: Groceries: one item's support
steps.task: This code should put the support of {yogurt} in yogurt_support and the rank of {tropical fruit} among the 169 items (1 = most common) in tropical_rank. Both come out wrong. Fix the two problems.
steps.starter:
data('Groceries', package = 'arules')

item_freq = arules::itemFrequency(Groceries)   # the support of every item, in the data's own order (not sorted)
item_freq |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(10)

yogurt_support = item_freq['Yogurt']
yogurt_support

tropical_rank = which(names(sort(item_freq)) == 'tropical fruit')
tropical_rank
steps.solution:
data('Groceries', package = 'arules')

item_freq = arules::itemFrequency(Groceries)   # the support of every item, in the data's own order (not sorted)
item_freq |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(10)

yogurt_support = item_freq['yogurt']
yogurt_support

tropical_rank = which(names(sort(item_freq, decreasing = TRUE)) == 'tropical fruit')
tropical_rank
steps.hint: Look at the item names in the top-10 output: are they capitalized? And which way does sort() order values unless you tell it otherwise?
steps.okMsg: Yogurt is in 13.95% of the baskets, and tropical fruit is the 8th most common item.

steps.title: Groceries: mine the rules
steps.task: Mine the Groceries rules with a minimum support of 0.01 and a minimum confidence of 50%, then keep the three rules found in the most baskets (the highest count) in top3. Run it first and read the error.
steps.starter:
data('Groceries', package = 'arules')

grocery_rules = arules::apriori(
  Groceries, parameter = list(
    support = 0.01, confidence = 50, minlen = 2)  )

arules::summary(grocery_rules)

top3 = arules::sort(grocery_rules, by = 'count', decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
arules::inspect(top3)
steps.solution:
data('Groceries', package = 'arules')

grocery_rules = arules::apriori(
  Groceries, parameter = list(
    support = 0.01, confidence = 0.5, minlen = 2)  )

arules::summary(grocery_rules)

top3 = arules::sort(grocery_rules, by = 'count', decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
arules::inspect(top3)
steps.hint: The error says confidence is not in [0,1]. Confidence is a share, like support: 50% is written as 0.5.
steps.okMsg: 15 rules. The one found in the most baskets, {other vegetables, yogurt} → {whole milk}, holds all three items in 219 baskets.

steps.title: Groceries: what does count tell you?
steps.prompt:
The three Groceries rules with the highest count (support 0.01, confidence 0.5):
> arules::sort(grocery_rules, by = 'count', decreasing = TRUE)[1:3] |> arules::inspect()
    lhs                                       rhs          support    confidence coverage   lift     count
[1] {other vegetables, yogurt}             => {whole milk} 0.02226741 0.5128806  0.04341637 2.007235 219
[2] {tropical fruit, yogurt}               => {whole milk} 0.01514997 0.5173611  0.02928317 2.024770 149
[3] {other vegetables, whipped/sour cream} => {whole milk} 0.01464159 0.5070423  0.02887646 1.984385 144
True or false: from this output, {other vegetables, yogurt} appears in exactly 219 baskets.
options: True
False
steps.why: False. 219 counts the baskets that hold all three items, {other vegetables, yogurt, whole milk}. So {other vegetables, yogurt} appears in at least 219 baskets. The coverage column gives the exact number: 0.04341637 × 9,835 = 427 baskets (or count / confidence = 219 / 0.5129).

steps.title: Groceries: confidence vs. lift
steps.prompt: In Groceries, the rule {soda} → {whole milk} has confidence 0.230 and lift 0.899. Across all 9,835 baskets, 25.6% have whole milk. Which statement is correct?
options: Baskets with soda are slightly less likely than the average basket to have whole milk.
Baskets with soda usually have whole milk, so this rule is a strong finding.
23% of all baskets have both soda and whole milk.
Of the baskets with whole milk, 23% also have soda.
A lift of 0.899 means 89.9% of soda baskets have whole milk.
steps.why: Lift below 1: soda baskets have whole milk 23.0% of the time, a bit less than the 25.6% of all baskets. The other choices mix up the measures: 23% is not most baskets; the share of all baskets with both is the support (4.0%); 23% is a share of the soda baskets, not of the whole-milk baskets (of those, 15.7% have soda); and lift is a ratio, not a percentage.

steps.title: Say the rule in words
steps.prompt: Here is one Groceries rule. In plain words, say what its confidence and its lift tell a store manager.

show.text:
lhs                          rhs          support    confidence coverage   lift     count
[1] {root vegetables, yogurt} => {whole milk} 0.01453991 0.5629921  0.02582613 2.203354 143

hints: Start from the baskets that hold root vegetables and yogurt.
Compare those baskets with all baskets.

title: Clustering and k-means
blurb: Grouping records with no outcome column, the k-means steps, and the practical issues: scaling, choosing k, and k-means in Tableau.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.html:
• Clustering puts records into groups so that records in a group are alike and records in different groups are not. There is no outcome column: it is descriptive data mining.
  • k-means, step by step. Step 0: pick k starting centers (often k random records). Step 1: each record joins its nearest center. Step 2: each center moves to the mean of its group. Repeat steps 1 and 2 until the centers stop moving.
  • What k-means makes small: the inertia, or within-cluster sum of squares: the sum of the squared distances from each record to its own center. Lower means tighter groups.
  • Practical issues. Rescale numeric columns first (z-scores, 0 to 1, or per-person rates), or the column with the biggest numbers decides the distance. Use more than one measure to choose k. Then visualize the clusters and try to explain who ended up where.
  • k-means in Tableau. Drag Cluster from the Analytics pane onto the view. Tableau runs k-means and colors each mark by its cluster.

steps.title: Salary and experience
steps.prompt: You run k-means on job postings using two columns: salary in dollars (about 40,000 to 200,000) and years of experience required (0 to 15). You do not rescale. What happens?
options: Salary decides almost all of the distance, so the clusters mostly split postings by salary
Experience decides the distance, since it is the smaller number
Both columns count equally, since k-means looks at each column separately
k-means stops with an error when columns are on different scales
steps.why: Distances add up squared differences, and a 10,000-dollar gap swamps a 5-year gap. Rescale both columns (for example, z-scores) so each one counts.

steps.title: Clustering in Tableau
steps.prompt: You have a Tableau scatter plot of penguins, bill length against flipper length. Where is Tableau's k-means clustering, and what does it do to the view?
options: In the Analytics pane: drag Cluster onto the view, and Tableau colors each mark by its cluster
In the Data pane: Cluster is a ready-made field you drag to Rows
In Show Me: Cluster is a chart type next to the scatter plot
Nowhere: Tableau cannot cluster, so you run k-means in R and import the groups
steps.why: Cluster sits in the Analytics pane, with Average Line, Trend Line and Forecast. Drop it on the view and Tableau runs k-means, then colors each mark by the cluster it joined.

steps.title: k-means in your own words
steps.prompt: Explain how the k-means algorithm groups records, step by step, and when it stops.
hints: What does k-means need before the first round?
Which center does a record belong to?
What happens to a center after its group is formed, and when does it end?
